Project Milestone #3  

Scenario 1: Infectious disease outbreak (simulated) in California

**1. Introduction**
This project uses simulated infectious disease outbreak data from Scenario 1 of the PHW251 Project Data GitHub repository to examine the distribution of infections across California.
Our primary research question is: How did infection rates during the outbreak vary by county, age, sex and race/ethnicity across California?

The datasets include simulated morbidity data from California and Los Angeles County, containing information on new infection cases and individual demographic and geographic characteristics.
Additionally, the analysis incorporates 2023 California Department of Finance population estimates. This dataset provide the denominators needed to calculate infection rates per 100,000 population, allowing for more meaningful comparisons across demographic and geographic groups.

By combining morbidity and population data, this project aims to identify variations in infection rates across California counties and demographic groups during the simulated outbreak.

**2. Import dataset**

```{r, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(gt)

#import datasets
getwd()
ca_pop <- read.csv("../phw251_projectdata/scenario_1/ca_pop_2023.csv")
sim_ca <- read.csv("../phw251_projectdata/scenario_1/sim_novelid_CA.csv")
sim_la <- read.csv("../phw251_projectdata/scenario_1/sim_novelid_LACounty.csv")

#clean the column names
ca_pop <- ca_pop %>%
  clean_names()
colnames(ca_pop)

sim_ca <- sim_ca %>%
  clean_names()
colnames(sim_ca)

sim_la <- sim_la %>%
  clean_names()
colnames(sim_la)

```

```{r, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}

# Identify all the variables in each dataset
sapply(ca_pop, class)
sapply(sim_ca, class)

```

Desired data types for analysis:

**4. Data Cleaning**

1) Convert variables

- Rename columns

```{r rename columns, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}

ca_pop <- ca_pop %>% rename(race_ethnicity = race7)

sim_la <- sim_la %>% rename(new_infections = dx_new,
                            race_ethnicity = race_eth,
                            age_cat = age_category)

sim_la <- sim_la %>%
  rename(
    cumulative_infected = infected_cumulative,
    new_unrecovered = unrecovered_new,
    cumulative_unrecovered = unrecovered_cumulative,
    new_severe = severe_new, 
    cumulative_severe = severe_cumulative
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    county = "Los Angeles"
  )

colnames(ca_pop)
colnames(sim_ca)
colnames(sim_la)
```

- Race/ethnicity

```{r convert race/ethnicity, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}

sim_ca <- sim_ca %>% mutate(
  race_ethnicity = case_when(
    race_ethnicity == 1 ~ "White NH",
    race_ethnicity == 2 ~ "Black NH",
    race_ethnicity == 3 ~ "AIAN NH",
    race_ethnicity == 4 ~ "Asian NH",
    race_ethnicity == 5 ~ "NHPI NH",
    race_ethnicity == 6 ~ "MR NH",
    race_ethnicity == 7 ~ "Hispanic"
    )
  )

unique(sim_ca$race_ethnicity)

sim_la <- sim_la %>%
  mutate(
    race_ethnicity = case_when(
      race_ethnicity == "White, Non-Hispanic" ~ "White NH",
      race_ethnicity == "Black, Non-Hispanic" ~ "Black NH",
      race_ethnicity == "American Indian or Alaska Native, Non-Hispanic" ~ "AIAN NH",
      race_ethnicity == "Asian, Non-Hispanic" ~ "Asian NH",
      race_ethnicity == "Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, Non-Hispanic" ~ "NHPI NH",
      race_ethnicity == "Multiracial (two or more of above races), Non-Hispanic" ~ "MR NH",
      race_ethnicity == "Hispanic (any race)" ~ "Hispanic",
      TRUE ~ race_ethnicity
    ))

unique(sim_la$race_ethnicity)

ca_pop <- ca_pop %>%
  mutate(
    race_ethnicity = recode(
      race_ethnicity,
      "WhiteTE NH" = "White NH"
    )
  )

unique(ca_pop$race_ethnicity)
```

- County names

```{r convert county names, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}

sim_ca$county <- str_remove(sim_ca$county, " County$")

unique(sim_la$county)
unique(sim_ca$county)
unique(ca_pop$county)

```

2) Recategorize age groups

```{r recategorize age groups}

ca_pop <- ca_pop %>%
  mutate(age_cat = case_when(
    age_cat %in% c("0-4", "5-11", "12-17") ~ "0-17",
    .default = age_cat)
  )

unique(ca_pop$age_cat)
unique(sim_ca$age_cat)
unique(sim_la$age_cat)

```

3) Standardize dates

```{r standarize date variables, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}

library(lubridate)
# Convert sim_ca date (YYYY-MM-DD)
sim_ca <- sim_ca %>%
  mutate(dt_diagnosis = ymd(dt_diagnosis))

# Convert sim_la date (DDMMMYYYY)
sim_la <- sim_la %>%
  mutate(dt_dx = dmy(dt_dx))

sim_la <- sim_la %>%
  rename(dt_diagnosis = dt_dx)

unique(sim_ca$dt_diagnosis)
unique(sim_la$dt_diagnosis)
```

\newpage

**5. Merge the datasets**

1) Combine sim_ca and sim_la in one dataset

```{r combine infection databases}

sim_combined <- bind_rows(
  sim_ca,
  sim_la
)

dim(sim_ca)
dim(sim_la)
dim(sim_combined)
```

2) Join population dataset

```{r join population dataset, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}

# summarize ca_pop dataset before merging
ca_pop_clean <- ca_pop %>%
  group_by(
    county,
    age_cat,
    sex,
    race_ethnicity
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    population = sum(pop, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

glimpse(ca_pop_clean)

# combine all datasets into one dataset
combined_df <- sim_combined %>%
  left_join(
    ca_pop_clean,
    by = c(
      "county",
      "age_cat",
      "sex",
      "race_ethnicity"
    ),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )

glimpse(combined_df)

```

\newpage

**6. Data analysis**

There are extra variables that we don't need in order to answer our research question. We simplified it to only include relevant information:

1) Select relevant information

```{r, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
selected_df <- combined_df %>%
  select(
    county,
    age_cat,
    sex,
    race_ethnicity,
    dt_diagnosis,
    new_infections,
    population
  )

glimpse(selected_df)
```

2) Check missing values

```{r}
# check missing values
colSums(is.na(selected_df))

# check invalid values
sum(selected_df$new_infections < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(selected_df$population <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# count unique strata with invalid population values (<= 0)
selected_df %>%
  filter(population <= 0) %>%
  distinct(county, age_cat, sex, race_ethnicity, population) %>%
  nrow()

```

3) Create new variables

- Create a month variable to examine monthly infection trends

```{r}
selected_df <- selected_df %>%
  mutate(diagnosis_month = month(dt_diagnosis, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)) %>%
  select(-dt_diagnosis)

head(selected_df)
```

- Calculate infection rates

```{r}
aggregated_df <- selected_df %>%
  group_by(county, age_cat, sex, race_ethnicity) %>%
  summarize(
    total_infections = sum(new_infections, na.rm = TRUE),
    population = first(population),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    infection_rate = if_else(
      population > 0,
      round(total_infections / population * 100000, 1),
      NA_real_
      )
    )

head(aggregated_df)
```


\newpage

**7. Data visualization**

Some observations had a population value of zero across multiple counties. Since population is used as the denominator when calculating infection rates, these observations cannot produce a valid rate. Therefore, observations with a population value of zero were excluded from the graphs and rate calculations only. The original dataset was retained without deleting these observations.

1) Monthly infection trend in California

```{r, fig.height = 4}
df_monthly <- selected_df %>%
  filter(population > 0) %>%
  group_by(diagnosis_month) %>%
  summarize(total_infections = sum(new_infections, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

df_monthly %>% gt()

ggplot(df_monthly,
       aes(x = diagnosis_month, y = total_infections)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Monthly New Infection Cases",
       subtitle = "California, 2023",
       x = "Month",
       y = "Number of New Infections") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

2) Infection rate by county

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
df_county <- aggregated_df %>%
  filter(population > 0) %>%
  group_by(county) %>%
  summarize(total_infections = sum(total_infections),
            population = sum(population),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    infection_rate = round
    (total_infections/population * 100000, 1)
         )

ggplot(df_county,
       aes(x = reorder(county, infection_rate), y = infection_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Infection rate by County",
       subtitle = "California, 2023",
       x = "County",
       y = "Infections per 100,000 Population") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

3) Infection rate by age group and sex

```{r, fig.height = 4}
df_age_sex <- aggregated_df %>%
  filter(population > 0) %>%
  group_by(age_cat, sex) %>%
  summarize(total_infections = sum(total_infections),
            population = sum(population),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    infection_rate = round
    (total_infections/population * 100000, 1)
         )

df_age_sex %>% gt()

ggplot(df_age_sex,
       aes(x = reorder(age_cat, infection_rate),
           y = infection_rate,
           fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel1",
                    labels = c("Female", "Male")) +
  labs(
    title = "Infection Rate by Age Group and Sex",
    subtitle = "California, 2023",
    x = "Age Group",
    y = "Infections per 100,000 Populations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
        )
```

**8. Data Dictionary**

1) Basic description provided for all variables
  - county: county names
  - age_cat: age category
    "0-17"
    "18-49"
    "50-64"
    "65+"  
  - sex: male/female
  - race_ethnicity: race/ethnicity categorization as defined by CA Dept of Finance 
    "White NH" = "White, Non-Hispanic"
    "Black NH" = "Black, Non-Hispanic"
    "AIAN NH" = "American Indian or Alaska Native, Non-Hispanic"
    "Asian NH" = "Asian, Non-Hispanic"
    "NHPI NH" = "Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, Non-Hispanic"
    "MR NH" = "Multiracial (two or more of above races), Non-Hispanic"
    "Hispanic" = "Hispanic (any race)"
  - new_infections: number of newly diagnosed individuals
  - population: CA Dept of Finance estimated all ages population for year 2023
  - diagnosis_month: the month when infections were diagnosed

3) Descriptive statistics (new infections, population)

```{r}
descriptive_stat <- selected_df %>%
  summarize(
    number_of_counties = n_distinct(county),
    number_of_age_categories = n_distinct(age_cat),
    number_of_race_ethnicity_categories = n_distinct(race_ethnicity),
    mean_infections = mean(new_infections, na.rm = TRUE),,
    median_infections = median(new_infections, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_infections = max(new_infections, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_population = mean(population, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_population = median(population, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
               names_to = "statistics",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 1))

descriptive_stat %>% gt()
```

3) Relationships and foundings
  
The four tables and graphs illustrate how the simulated infectious disease outbreak varied over time, geographically, and across demographic groups in California.

Monthly new infections increased steadily from May through September, reaching their peak in September before declining in October and November. This pattern suggests that the outbreak intensified throughout the summer months before beginning to subside in the fall.

County-level infection rates revealed geographic differences in disease burden. Imperial, Inyo, Kern, and Tulare counties had some of the highest infection rates per 100,000 residents. These counties generally have smaller populations than California's largest metropolitan counties, highlighting the importance of using population-adjusted infection rates rather than absolute case counts when comparing disease burden across geographic areas.

Infection rates by age group and sex showed consistent demographic patterns. Males experienced slightly higher infection rates than females across every age category. Additionally, infection rates increased progressively with age, with each successive age group experiencing a higher rate than the preceding group. This suggests that older populations experienced a greater burden of infection during the simulated outbreak, regardless of sex.

Together, these findings demonstrate that the simulated outbreak was not evenly distributed across California's population. While the monthly trends show when infections were most prevalent, the county and demographic analyses identify which populations experienced the highest infection rates.
